summary: This comparison covers two papers - one on chronic Lyme disease symptom burden and one on Long COVID quality of life - and does not describe either condition in general. Both papers separately report a gap between patient-reported experience and official diagnosis or surveillance figures, and both report worse health-related quality of life for the affected group than for a comparison population, though each uses its own distinct outcome measure that cannot be converted into the other's units. The Lyme disease paper is the only one of the two with direct out-of-pocket cost percentages, employment-loss figures, and diagnostic-delay percentages; the Long COVID paper is the only one with standardized EQ-5D/QALM quality-of-life metrics and comparisons to other chronic diseases. Neither paper supplies a total dollar cost of illness or caregiver-cost data. This is a small, non-random sample of one paper per condition, not a controlled study, so these patterns describe what these two specific papers happen to report, not the conditions as a whole.

This comparison covers two papers: the Lyme disease paper, built from a patient-registry chartbook, and the Long COVID paper, built from a peer-reviewed electronic-health-record phenotyping study. Both separately describe official counting methods producing lower or different counts than their own more detailed data sources, but the mechanisms differ: the Lyme disease paper points to insurance-claims exclusion of unbilled care, while the Long COVID paper points to diagnostic-code insensitivity. The Lyme disease paper offers detailed figures on diagnostic delay, access barriers, work loss, health status, and utilization that the Long COVID paper does not report, while the Long COVID paper offers detailed prevalence and chronicity figures with regional breakdowns that the Lyme disease paper does not attempt. Both papers explicitly state they lack the cost and subgroup detail needed to produce a validated total economic burden estimate. This analysis does not establish which condition carries a greater overall burden; it only shows what each paper, on its own terms, reports.

This comparison covers two papers - the Lyme disease paper (one persistent Lyme disease patient-registry chartbook) and the Long COVID paper (one BRFSS-based financial-hardship study) - and does not describe either condition in general. The Lyme disease paper is rich in diagnostic-delay, access-barrier, and healthcare-utilization detail but offers only one externally cited aggregate dollar figure rather than its own patient-level cost data. The Long COVID paper is rich in income- and education-stratified financial-hardship probabilities, with employment loss identified as a partial contributing channel, but contains no dollar costs, diagnostic-delay data, or access-barrier data at all. Where the two papers overlap, it is on the general idea that work/employment disruption contributes to burden and that both papers' figures are only partly disaggregated by demographic subgroup; elsewhere, the two papers largely cover different dimensions of burden rather than the same dimension measured differently.

This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper built from a 2021 self-selected clinician survey, and one Long COVID paper built from a qualitative interview study at a single academic clinic. The Lyme disease paper offers quantified clinician-reported cost and access-barrier figures, while the Long COVID paper offers only qualitative care-coordination and diagnostic-uncertainty findings with no cost data. Both papers separately describe a systemic gap in provider knowledge or guidelines for the condition studied, and both flag that their samples are small, non-random, and not broken down by subgroup. Because only one paper exists per condition here, this cannot show whether these patterns hold more broadly for either Lyme disease or Long COVID.

This comparison covers exactly two already-generated simulators - one built from a Lyme disease paper and one built from a Long COVID paper - and is not a controlled study of either condition. Both papers focus on how official diagnosis or surveillance counts compare to broader diagnosis-pattern data drawn from claims or EHR codes, but they measure this in different ways: the Lyme disease paper gives a specific numeric gap between a claims-based estimate and surveillance counts, while the Long COVID paper shows demographic and socioeconomic skew in who receives a diagnosis code plus a multi-year delay in that code's availability. Neither paper contains any cost, income-loss, or caregiving-burden data, so this comparison cannot address the financial burden of either condition. The patterns described here reflect only what these two specific uploaded documents report, not the conditions in general.

This comparison covers two papers: one Lyme disease paper built from a claims-based cohort study, and one Long COVID paper built from a privately insured claims cohort from the first pandemic year. Both papers report substantial direct medical cost increases associated with the condition studied, with costs rising sharply for more severe cases (disseminated Lyme disease or hospitalized COVID-19), and both explicitly state they do not measure indirect costs like lost income or caregiving. They differ in what kind of undercounting affects their official-data figures: the Lyme disease paper relies on an unvalidated claims-based case-classification algorithm, while the Long COVID paper had no specific diagnostic code available during its study period and used a proxy method the authors call a lower bound. Only the Lyme disease paper provides a specific out-of-pocket dollar figure and a multi-state annual cost extrapolation; the Long COVID paper's aggregate dollar figures are scoped only to its own study cohort. Because each simulator was built from a single uploaded document, this is not a controlled comparison of the two conditions, and no pattern here should be generalized beyond what each paper's own figures state.

This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease and one on Long COVID - and is not a controlled study comparing the conditions themselves. The Lyme disease paper focuses on diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis, work disability, and clinical-trial eligibility barriers using a patient registry, while the Long COVID paper tracks symptom persistence, work-productivity scores, and self-reported economic condition over 36 months in a Japanese hospitalized cohort. Both papers show work-related burden but measure it with different, non-convertible metrics, and neither reports any dollar-denominated cost figures. Both also pool their findings without demographic subgroup breakdowns. Several dimensions - diagnostic delay, claims-based undercounting, access barriers, and research-practice gaps - have evidence only in the Lyme disease paper, with nothing comparable reported in the Long COVID paper studied here.

This comparison covers two papers, one built from a 2009-2010 patient survey on chronic Lyme disease and one built from a 2025 electronic-health-record incidence study on Long COVID. The Lyme disease paper quantifies diagnostic delay, travel burden, hospital-access difficulty, and insurance or disability denial directly from patient-reported survey data, while the Long COVID paper quantifies excess incidence and clinical/demographic risk factors directly from EHR-based computable phenotypes. Neither paper reports direct dollar costs, out-of-pocket costs, or productivity-loss figures, and both flag unresolved issues with case definitions or guideline enforcement as a systemic limitation on their own findings. Because each paper uses a different data source, population, and measurement approach, the figures shown here describe what each paper separately reports and should not be read as a controlled comparison of the two conditions.

This comparison covers two papers: one Lyme disease paper, a historical cost-of-illness study of patients in five Maryland counties from 1997-2000, and one Long COVID paper, a diagnostic-phenotyping methods study from one Massachusetts health system. The Lyme disease paper supplies detailed dollar-cost figures that rise with disease stage and a nationwide cost extrapolation it flags as mismatched across price years and case definitions. The Long COVID paper supplies no cost figures at all, focusing instead on how a diagnosis-code-based count compares to an algorithm-based count and on demographic skew in who gets identified. The two papers share a pattern of flagging that their own official or coded counts can produce lower or different counts than an alternative method, and both present pooled headline figures without demographic subgroup breakdown. Because this pairing draws on one paper per condition, it cannot show whether these patterns hold more broadly for either condition.

This comparison covers two papers only - one Lyme disease paper reporting direct medical, non-medical, and productivity costs in 2019 euros, and one Long COVID paper reporting lost-labor/productivity costs in 2022 US dollars. Both papers present pooled national or population-level cost figures without demographic subgroup breakdowns, and both explicitly state that parts of total economic burden (such as long-term, caregiving, or direct medical costs) were left unmeasured. The two papers examine different cost categories, currencies, price years, and time windows, so their dollar figures cannot be added, divided, or otherwise combined into a single cross-condition number. Each paper also flags a different systemic gap specific to its own condition - a diagnostic-coding gap for Lyme disease and a lack of effective treatment for Long COVID. This is not a controlled study; it reflects only what these two independently built papers happen to report.

This comparison covers two papers: one Lyme disease paper that statistically reanalyzes four antibiotic retreatment trials and reports trial-level adverse-event rates, and one Long COVID paper that qualitatively interviews 21 patients about employment and income effects and offers illustrative income-loss scenarios. The two papers do not measure the same things: the Lyme disease paper's only quantified figures are adverse-event rates from clinical trials, while the Long COVID paper's only quantified figures are illustrative annual income-loss amounts and a cited external lost-wages estimate. Both papers independently note, in their own words, that the official processes they describe (treatment guidelines, diagnostic practice for accommodations) rest on evidence each paper itself calls insufficient. Because this is a comparison of exactly one paper per condition, with no cross-condition paper, these findings describe only these two papers and cannot be generalized to Lyme disease or Long COVID as conditions overall.

This analysis compares two papers -- one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper -- and does not describe either condition in general, since each group here consists of a single simulator. The Lyme disease paper documents sex-based differences in diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis with fatigue or psychiatric conditions, and self-reported functional impairment in a self-selected patient registry. The Long COVID paper documents objective, exercise-test-based work disability, sick-leave status, and ME/CFS overlap in a severity-selected occupational-disease cohort in Germany. Neither paper reports any dollar-denominated cost figures, so no cost comparison is possible from this evidence. Where both papers touch related ground -- diagnostic difficulty, work-related burden, demographic disaggregation -- they use different measurement tools and different populations, so the numbers should be read side by side rather than combined or treated as confirming each other.

This comparison covers two papers, one built from a European Lyme disease surveillance study and one built from a U.S. national Long COVID prevalence survey, and it does not describe either condition in general. The Lyme disease paper offers diagnostic-delay, hospitalization, and treatment-duration figures but no cost, insurance, or income-loss data, while the Long COVID paper offers national and demographic prevalence figures but no delay, severity, or cost data. The one shared pattern that can be shown with real figures is that both source documents are silent on direct and indirect costs, access barriers, and productivity loss. Because there is exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, and no paper covering both conditions, every row above reflects what these two specific documents happen to report rather than a broader claim about either condition.
